catalog_quote: 4.4.8. Tone The system is two tones plus downstep. There is downdrift, so that successive highs are progressively lowered by intervening lows. The Ẹrụwa tone system is discussed in Odumosu (1973:33-40). 4.4.9. Morphology There is no pluralization by prefix change. These and aspect in the verb are carried by a system of particles and tonal variation. [Elugbe 1989 'Edoid' chapter, p. 299] In SWE, Eruwa has two tones and a downstep; Isoko has two tones, no downstep, no upstep, and no downdrift (Elugbe 1977; Donwa 1982). [...] Tone plays a big role in the grammar of any Edoid language. With the possible exception of Epie-Atisa (see Thomas and Williamson 1967), verbs are not classified lexically by tone. As a result of that, perhaps, the role of tone in grammar is greater.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: There are five Edo languages called Southwestern Edo. They are Eruwa, Isoko, Okpẹ, Urhobo, and Uvbiẹ. [...] Isoko and Urhobo are the best known of the Southwestern Ẹdo languages, while the other three are often spoken of as dialects of these two: Eruwa, as a dialect of Isoko [...]. All these languages, none of which has extensive literature and little or none on tone, exhibit (with the exception of Ẹruwa, to judge by Odumosu [1973]) a phenomenon of final low tone raising.
new_statements.citation: Elugbe, Ben Ohi. 1977. Some implications of low tone raising in Southwestern Edo. Studies in African Linguistics, Supplement 7: 53-62.
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again., p.57 = journal p.53 (Elugbe 1977, sec.1 Introduction), rendered and read: the three quoted sentences are there; differences are only diacritics dropped in the report ('Ẹdo' for 'Edo', 'Ẹruwa' in the first sentence) and the marked ellipses. The rest of the paper (pp.53-62) analyses Isoko (Uzere) and Urhobo (Agbarho) only; Eruwa recurs only in the reference to Odumosu 1973. Nothing on stress/accent. So the compiler reading (tone language, no stress statement) is right, but the source chosen is a second-hand aside and the status is wrong, because the primary description IS open and already held by the project. new_statements.rule_in_words: Eruwa is treated, with its Southwestern Edoid sisters, as a level-tone language (the group has low and high tones, Isoko two tones plus final-low raising, Urhobo three); the only Eruwa-specific remark is that, per Odumosu 1973, it lacks the final low-tone raising of the others. No statement anywhere about word stress or accent in Eruwa.
new_statements.exceptions: Eruwa is the exception to SWE final low-tone raising (second-hand, after Odumosu 1973).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone/intonation of statements and citation forms in SWE generally; Eruwa itself is not analysed. The remark on Eruwa is explicitly second-hand ('to judge by Odumosu [1973]').
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to the same language: Eruwa = Erohwa = Ẹrụwa (Erakwa, Arokwa), ISO erh, Glottolog eruw1238, spoken in Erohwa village (Isoko South LGA, Delta State) and Anibeze (Sagbama LGA, Bayelsa). Often treated locally as a dialect of Isoko (isok1239) but classified as a separate Southwestern Edoid language by Elugbe. Not to be confused with Eruwa town (Ibarapa, Oyo State; Yoruba-speaking), which pollutes keyword searches.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Treats the five SWE languages (Eruwa, Isoko, Okpe, Urhobo, Uvbie) as tone systems; p.53: all exhibit final low-tone raising 'with the exception of Eruwa, to judge by Odumosu [1973]'. Analysis is of Isoko (2 tones + final-L raising) and Urhobo (3 tones); Eruwa data not presented.
